articles.title: Best Pickleball Paddles for Beginners (2026) — What to Buy First
articles.headline: Best Pickleball Paddles for Beginners (2026)
articles.metaDescription: The best beginner pickleball paddles in 2026. Why 16mm cores are more forgiving, what face material actually changes, and which paddles are worth your first purchase.

body.text: Buying a first pickleball paddle is harder than it should be. The same brand will sell you something at $40 and something at $250, and the marketing on both talks about carbon and cores without ever saying who should buy which. Here is the short answer: a beginner wants a 16mm core, a standard shape, and to spend well under $100. Everything below explains why, and what happens if you ignore that.
Skip the Wooden Paddles Entirely

Almost everyone's first experience of pickleball is with a wooden paddle from a cheap net set. They are heavy — often 10 or 11 ounces against a normal 8 — dead on contact, and they teach you to muscle the ball because nothing comes off the face on its own. Playing with one for a session is fine. Buying one is not. A basic composite paddle costs very little more and is a completely different object.
Core Thickness Is the Only Spec That Really Matters at First
Paddle cores come in roughly two thicknesses, and this single number changes more about how a paddle plays than the brand on the face.

items: 16mm cores flex more on contact. The ball stays on the face fractionally longer, which slows it down and makes dinks, drops and resets far easier to control. Off-centre hits still go where you intended.
13mm cores are firmer and punchier. The ball leaves faster, which is great for counter-attacking at the net if you already have the hands for it, and unhelpful if you do not.

body.text: If you are below a 4.0 rating, buy 16mm. The forgiveness shows up on every single mis-hit, and mis-hits are most of what a beginner does.
Face Material: What You Are Actually Paying For

Fibreglass faces are cheapest and give the most raw pop, which flatters a beginner's drives but makes soft shots harder to control. Graphite is calmer and more predictable — easier to place the ball. Raw carbon fibre has a gritty surface that holds the ball long enough to generate real spin, which is why every premium paddle now uses it. But raw carbon only pays off once you can deliberately brush up the back of the ball. Before that, you are paying for a feature you cannot yet use.

The default step-up recommendation for years and still the right answer for most people. The widebody shape gives one of the most forgiving sweet spots available, so shots struck away from centre still make it over the net with something on them. The Nomex core is firmer and louder than polymer, which means you get clear feedback about where on the face you actually hit it — genuinely useful while you are learning to control depth. It will not generate much spin, but nothing you should be buying at this stage will.

body.badge: Best First Paddle on a Budget
body.text: If you are not yet sure you will stick with pickleball, this is the sensible amount to risk. A graphite face over a polymer honeycomb core gives a soft, quiet response rather than the trampoline feel of the cheapest fibreglass paddles, and the standard shape keeps the sweet spot wide. It comes with a cover, which most paddles at this price do not. Treat it as a paddle to find out whether you love the sport, not one to grow into.

body.badge: Best If You Know You'll Stick With It
body.text: The first paddle here with a genuine 16mm core, and you feel it immediately in the soft game: dinks land shorter, resets stay down, and balls struck off-centre still behave. The hybrid shape adds a little reach over a standard paddle without narrowing the sweet spot the way a full elongated shape does. If you have played a few weeks and know this is your sport, skipping straight here saves you buying twice.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Buy the ONIX Graphite Z5 if you want the most forgiving paddle for the money. Buy the Niupipo if you are still deciding whether pickleball is for you. Buy the Selkirk SLK Evo if you already know you are staying and want a 16mm core you will not outgrow in a season. Do not buy a $200 carbon paddle as your first paddle — it will punish you for exactly the mistakes beginners make.
What About Grip Size?

Most paddles ship with a grip between 4.125 and 4.25 inches, which suits the majority of adult hands. The rule worth remembering is that you can always make a grip bigger by adding an overgrip, and it is very difficult to make one smaller. If you are between sizes, choose the smaller paddle and build it up. A grip that is too large forces you to squeeze harder, which is a direct route to elbow pain.

faq.q: How much should a beginner spend on a pickleball paddle?
faq.a: Somewhere between $40 and $100. Below $40 you are usually buying a wooden paddle or a very poor composite one. Above $100 you are paying for spin and shape characteristics that only help once your technique is repeatable. Most beginners are best served around the $70 to $90 mark.

faq.q: Is a heavier or lighter pickleball paddle better for beginners?
faq.a: Most beginners do best between 7.8 and 8.3 ounces. Lighter paddles are quicker to manoeuvre at the net but get pushed around by pace. Heavier paddles are more stable and generate more power with less effort, but slow your hands down in fast exchanges and can aggravate the elbow.

faq.q: Do I need a USAPA approved paddle?
faq.a: Only for sanctioned tournament play. For social and league play nobody checks. That said, essentially every paddle worth buying carries the approval anyway, so there is no reason to deliberately choose one that does not.

faq.q: How long before I should upgrade my paddle?
faq.a: Not until your shots are repeatable enough that you can feel what a paddle is doing. For most people that is six months to a year of regular play. Upgrading earlier tends to mean buying a paddle that demands cleaner contact than you can reliably produce.

faq.q: Can I use a table tennis or tennis racket for pickleball?
faq.a: No. A table tennis bat is far too small and a tennis racket is strung and much too large — neither is legal or playable. Pickleball paddles are a specific size and solid-faced, and there is no substitute.

articles.title: Pickleball Paddle Weight and Core Thickness Explained (2026)
articles.headline: Pickleball Paddle Weight and Core Thickness Explained
articles.metaDescription: How paddle weight and core thickness change the way a pickleball paddle plays. 13mm vs 16mm, light vs heavy, and how to pick without guessing.

body.text: Two numbers on a paddle spec sheet change how it plays more than anything else: weight and core thickness. Almost everything else — face material, shape, handle length — is a refinement on top of those. Get these two right and you will like almost any paddle. Get them wrong and no amount of carbon will save it.
Core Thickness: Control vs Pop
The core is the honeycomb layer sandwiched between the two faces. Thickness is usually 13mm or 16mm, and the difference is genuinely large.

items: 16mm — more flex, longer dwell time, softer response. Easier to control on dinks, drops and resets, and far more forgiving on off-centre contact. The default recommendation for anyone still developing a soft game.
13mm — firmer, faster off the face, more raw pop. Rewards players who can already redirect pace at the net. Less forgiving when you miss the middle.

body.text: The common mistake is assuming thinner means more advanced. It does not — plenty of very strong players use 16mm precisely because the control matters more than the extra pop. What thinner really means is less margin for error.
Weight: Stability vs Hand Speed
Most paddles land between 7.3 and 8.5 ounces. That sounds like a trivial range, and it is not — an ounce is very noticeable in a fast hands battle at the kitchen.

items: Under 7.8 oz (light) — fastest hands, easiest to manoeuvre, least strain on the arm. Gets pushed around by hard drives and gives you less free power.
7.8 to 8.3 oz (mid) — where most players should be. Enough mass to hold up against pace without slowing your hands noticeably.
Over 8.3 oz (heavy) — most stable and most free power on drives and overheads. Slower at the net and harder on the elbow over a long session.

body.text: Swing Weight Is the Number Nobody Prints

Two paddles can weigh the same on a scale and feel completely different, because it matters where the weight sits. An elongated paddle carries more of its mass away from your hand, so it feels heavier through the swing even at identical static weight. This is why an 8.0 oz elongated paddle can feel more tiring than an 8.2 oz standard one. If a paddle feels sluggish despite a reasonable weight, swing weight is usually why.

The reference point for a modern 16mm carbon paddle. The grit on the face holds the ball long enough that topspin rolls become a genuine weapon rather than a hopeful swipe, and the elongated head adds reach on the stretch and leverage on serves. The trade is a narrower sweet spot and higher swing weight — this paddle rewards clean contact and is unforgiving of lazy contact. Buy it once your technique is repeatable, not before.

A 16mm core in a hybrid shape, which keeps swing weight moderate while still adding a little reach. If you want the control benefits of a thick core without the tiring feel of a full elongated paddle, this is the shape to look at. A sensible landing spot for players who have decided they want control over raw power.

body.label: How to Choose Without Guessing
body.text: Start with core thickness: 16mm unless you specifically want a fast, punchy paddle for net exchanges. Then pick weight by what goes wrong in your game — if you get overpowered, go heavier; if you are late in hands battles, go lighter. Only then worry about shape, and remember that elongated adds reach at the cost of forgiveness and swing weight.
You Can Add Weight, But Not Remove It

Lead tape on the edge guard is a cheap and reversible way to add mass, and where you put it changes the feel: tape at 3 and 9 o'clock adds stability across the face, tape at 12 o'clock adds power and swing weight. What you cannot do is make a heavy paddle lighter. If you are unsure, buy at the lighter end of your range and add — it is the only direction that works.

faq.q: Is 13mm or 16mm better for pickleball?
faq.a: Neither is objectively better. 16mm gives more control, more dwell time and a bigger effective sweet spot, which suits most recreational and improving players. 13mm is faster off the face and better for players who counter-attack hard at the net. Most people should start at 16mm.

faq.q: What weight pickleball paddle should I use?
faq.a: Between 7.8 and 8.3 ounces suits the majority of players. Go lighter if you are frequently late in fast net exchanges or have any elbow trouble; go heavier if hard drives push your paddle around and you want more free power.

faq.q: Does a heavier paddle cause tennis elbow?
faq.a: It contributes. Heavier paddles transmit more shock and demand more from the forearm, and higher swing weight makes it worse. But the more common causes are a grip that is too small, a worn-out overgrip that makes you squeeze, and a paddle that is too stiff. Fix the grip before blaming the weight.

faq.q: What is swing weight and why does it matter?
faq.a: Swing weight measures how heavy a paddle feels while you move it, not how heavy it is on a scale. Mass positioned further from your hand raises it. Two paddles at identical static weight can feel very different because of it, which is why elongated shapes feel more tiring than standard ones.

faq.q: Can I add weight to a pickleball paddle?
faq.a: Yes — lead or tungsten tape on the edge guard is standard practice and fully reversible. Tape at 3 and 9 o'clock adds stability, tape at 12 o'clock adds power. You cannot make a paddle lighter, so buy light and add if you are unsure.

articles.title: Indoor vs Outdoor Pickleballs: The Difference Explained (2026)
articles.headline: Indoor vs Outdoor Pickleballs Explained
articles.metaDescription: Indoor and outdoor pickleballs are genuinely different balls. Hole count, wall thickness, flight and durability compared — and why using the wrong one ruins the game.

body.text: This is the single most common piece of confusion in pickleball, and unlike most gear debates it has a clear answer. Indoor and outdoor pickleballs are not interchangeable. They differ in hole count, wall thickness, weight and plastic formulation, and playing with the wrong one changes the game noticeably.
The Actual Differences

items: Outdoor balls have 40 small holes, thicker walls and more mass. The extra weight means wind pushes them around less, and the harder plastic makes them fly faster and hit harder.
Indoor balls have around 26 larger holes, thinner walls and softer plastic. They travel slower, are quieter, and take spin more readily because the softer surface grips the paddle face.

body.text: The practical result: an outdoor ball on a smooth gym floor skids, comes off the paddle faster than you expect and stings the hands. An indoor ball outdoors gets blown off line by any breeze and cracks quickly in cold weather. Neither is a small difference.
Why Outdoor Balls Crack So Often

Every pickleball is a single piece of moulded plastic being hit hard, repeatedly, often on abrasive concrete. Cracking is not a defect, it is the end of the ball's life. Cold makes it dramatically worse because the plastic becomes brittle — a ball that would last weeks in summer can split on a cold morning. If you play outdoors through winter, buy a ball specifically formulated to stay flexible at low temperatures.

The most widely played outdoor ball in the US and the official ball of the US Open, so if you enter tournaments this is likely what you will meet. One-piece construction means there is no seam to fail, and flight is genuinely consistent from ball to ball out of the pack. Durability in cold weather is its weak point, but at this price you buy a dozen and stop worrying about it.

The ball to buy if you play outdoors year round. The plastic formulation stays flexible at lower temperatures, which resists the brittle cracking that destroys cheaper balls on cold mornings. Flight is slightly softer than the X-40 and it holds its shape well through a long session. If you have been getting through balls faster than seems reasonable in winter, this is the fix.

A soft, quiet indoor ball that behaves predictably on a polished gym floor. The larger holes and thinner walls slow it noticeably compared to any outdoor ball, which is what makes long dink rallies possible and takes the sting out of hard drives. If your venue is a sports hall or church hall, this is what to bring.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Buy for the surface you actually play on, and do not try to make one ball do both jobs. Outdoors, the Franklin X-40 is the default and the ONIX Fuse G2 is the cold-weather answer. Indoors, the ONIX Fuse Indoor is the safe pick. If your club or league supplies balls, use theirs — consistency across a session matters more than brand preference.
When to Bin a Ball

As soon as it cracks, and before that if you can squeeze it noticeably out of round. A cracked ball does not just feel softer — it flies unpredictably, which quietly teaches you to compensate for something that is not your technique. Balls are consumable and cheap relative to everything else in the sport. Keeping a bad one in play is a false economy.

faq.q: Can I use an outdoor pickleball indoors?
faq.a: You can, but it plays badly. The heavier, harder outdoor ball skids on a smooth gym floor, comes off the paddle faster than expected and stings the hands. Most indoor venues have standardised on an indoor ball for exactly this reason.

faq.q: How many holes does an outdoor pickleball have?
faq.a: 40 small holes, against roughly 26 larger ones on an indoor ball. The smaller holes and thicker walls are what make outdoor balls heavier and more wind-resistant.

faq.q: How long does an outdoor pickleball last?
faq.a: Anywhere from a few sessions to a single cold morning. Abrasive courts and low temperatures are what kill them. Indoor balls last considerably longer because both the surface and the temperature are gentler.

faq.q: Are more expensive pickleballs actually better?
faq.a: Somewhat. Pricier balls tend to be more consistent between units and hold their shape longer, which matters in matches. But no ball is crack-proof, and the gap between a mid-priced and a premium ball is much smaller than the gap between using the right ball type and the wrong one.

faq.q: What colour pickleball is easiest to see?
faq.a: Whatever contrasts most with your court and background. Yellow and neon green are the safest outdoor defaults; on a dark indoor floor a lighter ball tracks better. Colour has no effect on flight, only on visibility.

articles.title: Best Pickleball Shoes for Beginners (2026) — Stop Using Runners
articles.headline: Best Pickleball Shoes for Beginners (2026)
articles.metaDescription: Why running shoes are dangerous for pickleball and what to buy instead. Court shoes compared for lateral support, outsole durability and wide fittings.

body.text: If you are going to spend money on one thing after a paddle, make it shoes. Running shoes are the most common piece of kit on a pickleball court and the most likely to hurt you: they are built to move you forwards, and pickleball moves you sideways on almost every point.
Why Running Shoes Are the Wrong Tool

A running shoe has a narrow, tall, soft midsole optimised for repeated forward impact. Load that sideways — which is exactly what a split step and a lateral shuffle do — and the whole shoe rolls over at the ankle. The outsole rubber is also compounded for road, not for the abrasion of a hard court, so it wears through fast. Court shoes sit lower, have a wider flatter base, a reinforced upper that resists lateral shear, and a non-marking sole.

The best-selling pickleball shoe in the US by volume, and it earns that on comfort. The midsole is noticeably plusher than anything else near this price, which is why it is the standard recommendation for players with knee complaints or anyone playing long social sessions. Lateral support is adequate rather than exceptional — this is a comfort shoe first — but it is a genuine court shoe and a very easy transition from trainers.

The pick if you would rather feel locked in than cushioned. It sits low to the ground with structured banding across the midfoot, so direction changes feel planted and there is very little roll at the ankle. The ride is firmer than the Skechers, which some people love and others find harsh after two hours. Available in a wide fitting, which matters more in court shoes than most people expect.

The cheapest option here that is genuinely a court shoe rather than a flat-soled trainer. The upper has a real support cage across the midfoot and the outsole is non-marking and flat enough to stay stable in a side shuffle. Cushioning is basic and it will not survive rough concrete for long, but as a first pair to get you out of running shoes it does the job that matters.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Any court shoe beats any running shoe. If you want comfort and play mostly socially, take the Skechers Viper Court. If you want stability and play competitively, take the K-Swiss Express Light. If money is tight, the FILA Volley Zone is a real court shoe at a low price. And if you have wide feet, buy a wide fitting rather than sizing up — court shoes are cut deliberately narrow.
Indoor and Outdoor Wear Very Differently

Outdoor courts are concrete or asphalt and destroy soft outsoles in weeks. Indoor gym floors are far gentler but demand a genuinely non-marking sole that grips polished wood. If you play mostly outdoors, prioritise outsole durability above everything else — some manufacturers offer an outsole guarantee, which tells you exactly where they expect the wear to happen.
Replace Them Before They Look Finished

The support in a court shoe fails before the upper looks worn out. If the midsole has compressed flat, or you can twist the shoe easily along its length, the lateral support has gone even if there is tread left. Playing three or four times a week outdoors, six to nine months is realistic. Judging by appearance will keep you in a shoe that stopped protecting you months ago.

faq.q: Can I wear running shoes for pickleball?
faq.a: You can, but you should not. Running shoes have tall, soft, narrow midsoles designed for forward motion, and they roll at the ankle under the lateral load pickleball creates on every point. Rolled ankles and rapidly shredded outsoles are both avoidable with a proper court shoe.

faq.q: Are tennis shoes good for pickleball?
faq.a: Yes — they are the closest thing there is. Tennis and pickleball make almost identical demands: lateral movement, hard stops, abrasive hard courts. Many dedicated pickleball shoes are lightly modified tennis shoes. If you already own tennis shoes, use them.

faq.q: Do I need wide pickleball shoes?
faq.a: If you normally buy wide shoes, yes. Court shoes are cut narrow on purpose so your foot does not slide inside the shoe during lateral moves. Sizing up in a standard width is the wrong fix — it adds length without adding width where you actually need it.

faq.q: How often should I replace pickleball shoes?
faq.a: Every six to nine months if you play three or four times a week outdoors, and longer indoors. Judge by support rather than tread: if the shoe twists easily or the midsole feels dead and flat, the protection has gone regardless of how the outsole looks.

faq.q: What is the difference between indoor and outdoor pickleball shoes?
faq.a: Mostly the outsole rubber. Outdoor shoes use a harder, abrasion-resistant compound with a more aggressive tread to survive concrete. Indoor shoes use a softer gum-style non-marking rubber that grips polished wood. Outdoor shoes work indoors but can feel slippery; indoor shoes wear out fast outside.

articles.title: Pickleball Gear for Beginners (2026) — The Complete Starter Guide
articles.headline: Pickleball Gear for Beginners: The Complete Guide
articles.metaDescription: Everything a new pickleball player actually needs, in order of priority. Paddle, shoes, balls, grips and what you can safely skip at the start.

body.text: Pickleball is one of the cheapest racket sports to start, which is part of why it grew so fast. You need a paddle, a ball and court shoes, and that is genuinely it. This guide covers what to buy in order of priority, and — just as usefully — what you can ignore for the first year.
1. A Paddle (Buy This First)

The paddle is the only thing that changes how the game feels in your hand. Buy a 16mm core in a standard or hybrid shape, with a graphite or fibreglass face. Do not buy a wooden paddle from a net set, and do not buy a $250 carbon paddle as your first purchase — it demands cleaner contact than a beginner can reliably produce.

Forgiving, widely available and the most common step-up recommendation in the sport. The widebody shape gives a large sweet spot, and the firmer core gives clear feedback about where you actually struck the ball, which is genuinely useful while you are learning depth control. Not a spin paddle, but an excellent one to develop touch on.
2. Court Shoes (Buy This Second)

This matters more than most beginners expect. Pickleball is lateral, and running shoes roll at the ankle under sideways load. A court shoe sits lower, has a wider base and a reinforced upper. If you are going to play more than once a week, this is the purchase most likely to keep you playing rather than resting an injury.

Plush enough that it does not feel like a punishment after running shoes, while still being a genuine court shoe with a flat, stable base and non-marking sole. Available in wide fittings. If you are unsure whether you will play enough to justify proper shoes, this is the low-regret option.
3. Balls (Cheap, and You Will Need More Than You Think)

Buy for the surface you play on: 40-hole outdoor balls outside, 26-hole indoor balls in a sports hall. They are consumable — outdoor balls crack, especially in cold weather — so buy a multipack rather than three at a time. A cracked ball flies unpredictably and quietly teaches you to compensate for something that is not your technique.

The most widely played outdoor ball in the US and the official US Open ball. Consistent flight out of the pack and cheap enough to buy by the dozen, which is the right way to buy pickleballs. If you play outdoors, start here and only change if you are cracking balls in cold weather.
4. An Overgrip (The Best Few Pounds You Will Spend)

An overgrip fixes a slippery handle, lets you build up a grip that is slightly too small, and gets replaced when it wears instead of the paddle. If your hands sweat, a dry-feel grip such as Tourna gets grippier as it absorbs moisture — the opposite of a tacky grip, which turns slick. Replace it every three or four weeks; a slipping handle makes you squeeze, and squeezing causes elbow pain.

The grip most players with sweaty hands end up on. It feels chalky and slightly rough when new, which puts some people off immediately, but it becomes grippier as it absorbs sweat rather than slicker. Thin, so it barely changes handle size. Cheap, and sold in multipacks — which is how overgrips should be bought.

body.label: The Minimum Viable Kit
body.text: A 16mm paddle, a pair of court shoes, a multipack of the right balls for your surface, and an overgrip. That is a complete pickleball setup and it does not cost much. Everything else — bags, nets, covers, sunglasses — is genuinely optional and can wait until you know how often you are actually going to play.
What You Can Safely Skip at First

items: A net. Almost everyone plays at a club, park or sports hall where nets already exist. Only buy one if you have a driveway and intend to play at home.
A tour bag. A sling bag or any small backpack carries two paddles and a bottle. Bag size should follow your routine, not your ambitions.
A second paddle. Useful for tournaments where a crack ends your day. Irrelevant for social play.
A paddle cover. Worth it once you own a raw carbon paddle. Unnecessary on a painted budget face.

body.text: The Order That Actually Matters

If you have limited money, spend it in this order: shoes, paddle, balls, grip. That is deliberately not the order most people buy in — the paddle is more exciting — but shoes are the item that prevents injury, and an injury costs more playing time than any paddle upgrade ever gains you.

faq.q: How much does it cost to start playing pickleball?
faq.a: A workable setup — a decent paddle, court shoes, a multipack of balls and an overgrip — lands in the region of $150 to $250 depending on the shoes. You can start for less by using tennis shoes you already own and a cheaper paddle.

faq.q: What do I actually need to play pickleball?
faq.a: A paddle, a ball and shoes you can move sideways in. Courts and nets are usually provided wherever you play. Everything else is optional and most of it can wait until you know how often you will play.

faq.q: Should I buy a pickleball set with paddles and a net?
faq.a: Generally no. The paddles in those sets are usually wood and heavy, and the nets are the weakest part. If you want a net for a driveway, buy the net separately and buy proper paddles — you will end up replacing the set paddles almost immediately.

faq.q: Do I need different gear for indoor and outdoor pickleball?
faq.a: Balls, yes — definitively. Shoes, somewhat: outdoor courts wear outsoles far faster, so durability matters more. Paddles are the same for both. If you play on both surfaces, keep two types of ball and pick shoes based on wherever you play most.

faq.q: How long does pickleball gear last?
faq.a: Paddles soften after 12 to 24 months of regular play. Court shoes last six to nine months outdoors. Overgrips need replacing every three or four weeks. Balls are the fastest consumable of all, especially outdoors in cold weather.

articles.title: Pickleball vs Tennis Gear: What Transfers and What Doesn't (2026)
articles.headline: Pickleball vs Tennis Gear: What Transfers
articles.metaDescription: Coming to pickleball from tennis? Which gear carries over, which does not, and why your tennis shoes are fine but your racket and balls are not.

body.text: A lot of people arrive at pickleball from tennis, and the natural question is how much of the existing kit bag still works. The short answer: shoes, bags and grips transfer almost completely. Rackets and balls do not transfer at all.
What Transfers Directly

items: Shoes. Tennis shoes are the closest thing to a pickleball shoe there is — both sports demand lateral stability, hard stops and abrasion-resistant outsoles. Many dedicated pickleball shoes are lightly modified tennis shoes.
Bags. A tennis bag carries paddles happily. The only difference is that pickleball paddle sleeves are shorter and better shaped, so paddles slide around less.
Overgrips. Identical product. Tourna, Wilson Pro and HEAD Xtremesoft are used across both sports with no modification at all.
Court sense. Not gear, but worth saying: the split step, the volley technique and the movement patterns carry over more than the equipment does.

body.text: What Does Not Transfer

A tennis racket is strung, far larger and completely illegal in pickleball — there is no substitute, and no adaptation. Tennis balls are heavier, pressurised and bounce far higher; a pickleball is a moulded plastic ball with holes and behaves nothing like one. And a tennis net is 42 inches at the posts against pickleball's 36, and wider than the court, so a tennis net cannot simply be reused unless the facility has an adjustable system.

A tennis shoe, and the most durable option on our pickleball shoe list — which neatly makes the point about how much the two sports share. The outsole compound is built for players who wear through soles in weeks, and the series carries an outsole guarantee. Heavier than a dedicated pickleball shoe and it takes a few sessions to break in, but if abrasive courts are eating your shoes it is the answer in either sport.
The Adjustment Tennis Players Find Hardest

It is not the gear, it is the paddle having no strings. A tennis racket's string bed does an enormous amount of work generating spin and absorbing pace. A solid paddle face does neither, which is why tennis players often arrive hitting long for the first few sessions — the shots that a string bed would have brought down simply do not come down. This is also why paddle face material matters so much in pickleball: it is the only source of grip on the ball.

If you are used to generating spin with a string bed, a raw carbon face is the closest a paddle gets. The grit holds the ball long enough that brushing up the back of it produces genuine topspin, and the elongated shape gives leverage on serves that feels more familiar coming from tennis. It is unforgiving of poor contact, which is the trade — but tennis players tend to have the contact quality to justify it sooner than complete beginners.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Keep your tennis shoes, your bag and your overgrips. Buy a paddle and the right balls for your surface, and expect the ball to fly longer than your instincts predict for the first few sessions. Do not try to adapt a racket or reuse tennis balls — neither works, and neither is legal.
One Genuine Warning

Tennis players often start pickleball assuming it is gentler and therefore safer. The rallies are shorter and the court is smaller, but the direction changes are sharper and more frequent, and a lot of play happens at the kitchen line with very little reaction time. Court shoes matter just as much here as they do in tennis, and possibly more.

faq.q: Can I use tennis shoes for pickleball?
faq.a: Yes, and they are the best substitute there is. Tennis and pickleball make near-identical demands on a shoe: lateral stability, hard stops, and outsoles that survive hard courts. What you should not use is a running, walking or gym trainer.

faq.q: Can I use a tennis racket for pickleball?
faq.a: No. A tennis racket is strung and far too large, and it is not legal in any form of pickleball. Paddles are solid-faced and a specific size. There is no adaptation that works.

faq.q: Are tennis balls and pickleballs interchangeable?
faq.a: Not at all. A tennis ball is pressurised, felt-covered and bounces much higher; a pickleball is moulded plastic with holes and a low, quick bounce. The two play nothing alike and pickleball rules require a proper pickleball.

faq.q: Is a tennis net the right height for pickleball?
faq.a: No. A tennis net is 42 inches at the posts; pickleball is 36 at the posts and 34 at centre, on a narrower court. Some facilities have adjustable systems, but usually the answer is a portable pickleball net set up inside the tennis court.

faq.q: Why do tennis players hit long in pickleball at first?
faq.a: Because a paddle has no string bed. In tennis, the strings generate spin that brings the ball down inside the baseline. A solid paddle face produces far less spin, so shots that would have dipped in tennis carry long until you adjust your swing path and pace.
